doc.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Leaving the Navy and keeping to his own style amid bebop
summary: Out of the Navy in 1945, back to Hudson; Terry did not copy bebop but admired it.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: And that’s when you went back to St. Louis.
Then that’s when you hooked up with the Hudson band and [ ? ? ].
When did you first start getting into the more modern ideas?

I suppose when I first started listening to it, when it first became on the scene. I never was one to really jump up and copy things, but I would love the way it sounded. I was always browbeaten by some of the people who would talk to me. They said,

“Believe in what you’re doing. Just study and stick to what you’re doing, but master your instrument.” So I’d work on – diligently at maintaining whatever ability I had to do whatever the heck it was, but I’m glad that I wasn’t the type to just jump and get on the bandwagon and end up sounding like a poor man’s Dizzy Gillespie or something. At least I tried to stick with what it was that I was capable of doing.
